chunks: "An analog signal is continuous: it can take any value in a range, and it can change at any moment.
A thermocouple voltage or a microphone output is analog, and its exact value carries the information.
A digital signal only has a few allowed levels, usually two, and the information is in which level you are at when you look, not the exact voltage.
The big payoff of digital is noise immunity. If a logic high is anything above, say, 2 volts on a 3.
3 volts part, then a few hundred millivolts of noise doesn't change the answer, and a receiver can regenerate a clean edge. Analog noise just adds into the signal permanently.
Digital also lets you copy, store and process data perfectly, and use the same cheap CMOS process for everything. The costs are bandwidth and resolution.
Digitizing an analog signal means sampling it in time and quantizing it in amplitude, so you throw away some information, and you need an ADC and DAC at the edges.
Also, a digital wire is still analog underneath: if the edge is too slow, rings, or crosses the threshold region, it'll misbehave.
So I think of digital as analog signals that I've agreed to only look at in two places."
